title: "Debiasing Argo Box Averages with a Simulated Sampling Propensity"
jupyter: python3
fig-dpi: 300

## The problem

Argo floats drift with the ocean currents, so where they take profiles is not uniform in space
and time. If floats tend to collect in cold (or warm) water, then the simple average of their
profiles is a biased estimate of the box's average ocean heat content (OHC), even with no
measurement error. Our aim is to measure that bias and remove it.

**Setting.** There are two boxes in the North Atlantic, Box A ($22$–$34^\circ$N) and Box B
($34$–$45^\circ$N), both spanning $60$–$40^\circ$W. We also use their union, A $\cup$ B. We work in
the years 2015–2019. We use the GLORYS12 reanalysis as "truth": it gives the OHC anomaly $Z$
($0$–$2000$ m, seasonal cycle and trend removed) on every $1/12^\circ$ cell on every day. The
**target** is the true box-year mean, $Z$ averaged over the box's ocean area $A$ and the year's
$T$ days:
$$
\bar Z \;=\; \frac{1}{|A|\,T}\int_{\text{year}}\int_{A} Z(s,t)\,ds\,dt .
$$
Here $x=(s,t)$ is a location and day, and $|A|\,T$ is the box's area-time (area times days).

## The sampling propensity

Imagine re-running the Argo program many times, with the same deployment strategy and the same
ocean currents but different individual launches. The **sampling propensity** $q(x)$ at a place and
day $x$ is the *average number of profiles per unit area per day* that would land there. A high
$q$ means the location is routinely oversampled, and a low $q$ means it is routinely undersampled.
It is set by two things: where and when floats are deployed, and where the currents carry them
afterwards. Formally,
$$
q(x)\,\Delta A\,\Delta t \;\approx\; \mathbb E\big[\#\text{ profiles in a small patch of area }\Delta A\text{ and duration }\Delta t\text{ around }x\big],
$$
where the expectation is over re-runs of the program. The one fact we need follows from this: for
any function $f$, a sum over the profiles $x_i$ averages to an integral weighted by $q$,
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\sum_i f(x_i)\Big] \;=\; \int f(x)\,q(x)\,dx . \tag{1}
$$

**Why the simple mean is biased.** Applying (1) to the numerator and denominator of the simple mean
$\hat Z_{\text{mean}}=\frac1n\sum_i Z(x_i)$ over the $n$ profiles in the box-year gives
$$
\mathbb E\big[\hat Z_{\text{mean}}\big] \;\approx\; \frac{\int_{\text{box-year}} Z\,q\,dx}{\int_{\text{box-year}} q\,dx}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\text{bias} \;\approx\; \frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{\text{box-year}}(q,\,Z)}{\operatorname{mean}_{\text{box-year}}(q)} .
$$
So the simple mean is a $q$-weighted average of $Z$, not the plain average. It is biased exactly
when $q$ lines up with $Z$: if floats are routinely denser where $Z$ is low, the average runs
low.

## Estimating the propensity by simulation

We cannot re-run the real Argo program, but we can simulate it.

1. **Deployments.** A simulated array resamples the real 2010–2019 Argo deployments in the region
   (with replacement, within each year, keeping each float's lifespan). Each launch is nudged by up
   to $\pm1/12^\circ$ and $\pm10$ days.
2. **Drift.** Each float is advected at its $1000$ m parking depth through GLORYS daily currents and
   reports a profile every $10$ days. The years 2010–2014 are a spin-up, so the array is mature by
   2015.
3. **Repeat.** We build $R = 1000$ independent simulated arrays.

Pooling all their profiles, let $C(c)$ be the average number of profiles per array in cell-day
$c$ (a $1/12^\circ$ cell on one day), and $a(c)$ its area of ocean deeper than the $1000$ m parking depth
times one day (zero after the simulation ends). With Gaussian smoothing weights $G$, standard deviation $\sigma_s\approx17$ km
($1/6^\circ$) in space and $\sigma_t=4$ days in time,
$$
\hat q(c) \;=\; \frac{\sum_{c'} G(c-c')\,C(c')}{\sum_{c'} G(c-c')\,a(c')},
\qquad
C(c) \;=\; \frac1R\sum_{r=1}^{R} \#\{\text{profiles of array } r \text{ in } c\}.
$$
This is smoothed profiles divided by smoothed ocean area-time, in profiles per unit area per day.
Dividing by the *smoothed* area, rather than the area of one cell, keeps the estimate from being
dragged down near coasts and the edge of the record, where part of the kernel falls on land or
outside the record.

**Why this bandwidth.** It is a trade-off between noise and resolution:

* **Noise.** Each kernel holds about $70$ simulated profiles, so $\hat q$ is precise to about
  $12$%.
* **Resolution.** It is about ten times finer than the scales on which $Z$ varies (a few hundred km
  and one to four months), and fine enough to resolve eddy-scale trapping.

Binning to cells first is only a speed-up: evaluating the kernel at the exact profile positions
changes the results below by less than $0.001$ GJ m$^{-2}$.

## The realized bias of the simple mean

For simulated array $r$, we read the true $Z$ at each of its $n_r$ profiles $x_i$ inside a
box-year and average them:
$$
\hat Z_{\text{mean},r} \;=\; \frac1{n_r}\sum_{i=1}^{n_r} Z(x_i),
\qquad
B_r \;=\; \hat Z_{\text{mean},r} - \bar Z .
$$
$B_r$ is the **realized bias** of array $r$. Because GLORYS is complete, $\bar Z$ is known exactly,
and the only source of error is where the floats happened to sample.

A single array's $B_r$ mixes two things: a systematic part from the propensity, and luck of the
draw. The average over arrays, $\bar B=\frac1R\sum_r B_r$, isolates the systematic part, the
**sampling bias**, which is what the estimators below are designed to remove. Its Monte Carlo
standard error is $\mathrm{sd}(B_r)/\sqrt R$. The spread of $B_r$ across arrays is the luck.

## Debiasing: weight each profile by $1/\hat q$

The fix is the survey-sampling idea of inverse-probability weighting. A profile in an
undersampled place (low $\hat q$) stands in for more ocean, so it gets more weight. Each profile
gets weight $v_i = 1/\hat q(x_i)$, the area-time it represents. With $Z_i=Z(x_i)$:

* **Horvitz–Thompson (HT):**
  $$
  \hat Z_{\text{HT}} \;=\; \frac{1}{|A|\,T}\sum_i \frac{Z_i}{\hat q(x_i)} .
  $$
  By (1) with $f=Z/q$, $\;\mathbb E\big[\sum_i Z_i/q(x_i)\big]=\int Z\,dx=|A|\,T\,\bar Z$, so HT is
  unbiased when $\hat q=q$. It relies on $\hat q$ having the right overall level.
* **Hájek:**
  $$
  \hat Z_{\text{H}} \;=\; \frac{\sum_i Z_i/\hat q(x_i)}{\sum_i 1/\hat q(x_i)} ,
  $$
  the weighted average. It replaces the known area-time $|A|\,T$ with its own estimate
  $\sum_i 1/\hat q(x_i)$. Only the *relative* propensity matters, because any overall scale error
  in $\hat q$ cancels. This is usually the more robust choice.

For each estimator we compute the same realized bias $B_r$ per array, and report the **percent of
the simple mean's bias removed**, $100\,\big(1-\bar B_{\text{est}}/\bar B_{\text{mean}}\big)$.

In this validation, each simulated array is weighted by the $\hat q$ built from all $1000$ arrays.
Leaving the array's own profiles out of $\hat q$ changes the Hájek estimate by at most
$0.02$ GJ m$^{-2}$.

**Takeaways.**

* The simple mean is biased low in Box B in every year, by $0.23$–$0.42$ GJ m$^{-2}$. Floats
  collect over colder water. In Box A the bias is smaller and its sign varies from year to year.
* Hájek weighting removes about $89$% of the bias in Box B and in A $\cup$ B, and about $81$% in
  Box A (pooled over years). What remains is about $-0.03$ GJ m$^{-2}$ in Box B, roughly a tenth
  of the original.
* HT does slightly worse. The weights sum to only about $93$% of the box, and that scale error
  shows up wherever $\bar Z$ is large. Hájek cancels it.
* Weighting also halves the typical error of a single array's five-year Box B average, from
  $0.37$ to $0.19$ GJ m$^{-2}$, because bias dominated the simple mean's error there. For
  single years the reduction is 17–28%.

## What this does and does not show

This is a best case. The profiles are generated by exactly the same process that $\hat q$ was
estimated from, so the result shows that the *estimators* work when the propensity is right. For
real Argo, $\hat q$ must also describe where **real** floats go. Real trajectories drift away from
GLORYS-advected ones within weeks, and a first check with an earlier $\hat q$ found that, on the GLORYS
field, the real array's Hájek bias in Box B stays close to its simple-mean bias. Checking and correcting $\hat q$ for the real array is the next step.
